items.name: Nigeria
items.overview: Most of our Nigeria region is tropical, with distinct wet and dry seasons. Civilizations such as the Maninka kingdoms and the Benin Empire thrived here for centuries, relying on the vast river systems and extensive coastline for fishing and trade. Alongside colonial languages like French and English, Indigenous languages are widely spoken and are sometimes the local lingua franca, as is the case of Yoruba and Hausa. Today, many cultural expressions, such as food and music, reflect a blend of European and African influence, while others, including storytelling, sculpture, and textiles, remain distinctly West African.
items.alsoLocated: Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, Sierra Leone

items.name: Mali
items.overview: The core of our Mali region extends from the heart of the Sahara Desert to the tropical coasts of Sierra Leone. Mali has been an important crossroads on the trade routes between North Africa and West Africa for centuries. Along with goods, traders brought religion, and the cities of Djenné and Timbuktu and their mosques are evidence of early and longstanding Islamic influence. Bambara, a Niger-Congo language, is the most common spoken language, and Mali’s oral literature, woodcarving, pottery, and textiles—including the bògòlanfini dyeing process—are recognized far beyond the country’s borders.
items.alsoLocated: Cote D'Ivoire, Gambia, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Niger, Senegal

items.name: Ivory Coast & Ghana
items.overview: Early French and Portuguese explorers identified sections of the West African coast by the area’s resources, which is how Côte d'Ivoire, or Ivory Coast, got its modern name. Neighboring Ghana was known as the Gold Coast until it won independence from colonial rule in 1957 and renamed itself after a medieval West African empire. Today, more than 46 million people live in the two countries, which depend less on gold and ivory than they do chocolate: Ivory Coast and Ghana produce more than half of the world’s cocoa.

items.name: Benin & Togo
items.overview: Our Benin & Togo region centers around the Dahomey Gap, a strip of savanna that divides the region’s otherwise humid rainforest in two. The area has been home to both vast kingdoms and societies. Dozens of ethnic groups that live here, including the Ewe, the Gun, and the Weme, as well as the arrival of French and British colonizers, have shaped the region’s societies and cultures. Food staples such as yams, cassava, and fish, and art forms including wooden sculptures and colorful kente cloth remain emblematic of this part of West Africa.

items.name: Cameroon
items.overview: Our Cameroon region boasts a rich tapestry of landscapes, from beaches and deserts to mountains, grasslands, and rainforest. The people are as diverse as the landscape. Many speak four or more languages. They practice Christianity, Islam, and animist religions, or a hybrid of two or more. Hospitality is important, especially sharing food with visitors. Bikutsi and Makossa are two of the region’s popular music styles, and music and dance are common ways to mark festive occasions, including holidays, weddings, coronations, and births.
items.alsoLocated: Angola, Burundi, Gabon, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, Seychelles, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia, Zimbabwe

items.name: Nigerian Woodlands
items.overview: Our Nigerian Woodlands region lies just north of the confluence of the Niger and Benue rivers, extending northward to where the woodland meets the savanna. Both the Hausa and Fulani ethnic groups wield a strong influence on the culture. Trade with North Africa introduced Islam, while later British rule brought Christianity. Both religions are still practiced today and have been influenced by longstanding Indigenous religions. In many areas, religion and art are closely intertwined: dance, sculpture, woodcarving, and storytelling are all popular art forms that are often imbued with spiritual significance.

items.name: Egypt
items.overview: Occupying the northeastern corner of the African continent, our Egypt region lies between Libya in the west and the Red Sea in the east. Most of the country is desert, so 96% of the population lives in the fertile Nile Valley, where nearly all urban centers are located. Historically, it is known for its pharaonic period, which left such famed icons as the Pyramids of Giza and the Sphinx. Following the 7th century Islamic conquest, Egypt became the capital of several powerful Muslim dynasties that fostered arts, literature, and the sciences.

items.name: Central Nigeria
items.overview: Our Central Nigeria region is centered on the confluence of the Niger and Benue Rivers, reaching north into Niger and southeast into Cameroon. Historically, the area was home to diverse ethnic groups that formed distinct kingdoms and societies. The arrival of North African traders and, later, European colonizers reshaped cultural divisions and political boundaries. Today, while Nigerians maintain their distinct ethnic identities and local languages, many in this region share cultural and spiritual practices, such as subsistence farming, bride prices, lavish weddings celebrated with music and dance, and venerating ancestors.

items.name: Nilotic Peoples
items.overview: Nilotic peoples are linked by a common language and homelands along the Nile Valley in Sudan in the distant past. Over time, groups moved southward into East Africa and as far south as Tanzania. They include the Luo, Maasai, Turkana, Dinka, Nuer, and Kipsigis. Some became farmers and fishers over time; others have remained nomadic pastoralists, keeping herds of cattle and goats. With the end of colonialism, they’ve entered government and business and have gained fame as the world’s greatest distance runners.

items.name: North-Central Nigeria
items.overview: From the tropical savannas of Nigeria to the arid Sahel in southern Niger, our North-Central Nigeria region boasts a rich history spanning millennia. Pastoralists eventually gave way to grain farmers, and northern Nigeria became an important trade hub connecting North Africa with the West African coast. Traders exchanged weapons, beads, coral, cloth, and spices. In time, trade routes also introduced Islam, which influenced politics, law, and architecture. Islam remains a uniting factor in the north, as does Hausa, the oldest known written language in West Africa, which many people speak along with one or more local languages.

items.name: Twa
items.overview: Dense tropical forests dominate our Twa region. Highly organized kingdoms thrived amidst the forests, adept at administration, trade, and education despite their isolation. Over two hundred ethnic and linguistic groups make their homes here, and many people are fluent in multiple languages. The earliest contact with outside traders came via the Congo River, which brought European missionaries and colonizers to the region. Despite colonial influence, villagers remain connected by longstanding traditions of generosity, spiritual ties to animal totems, and festive celebrations that include brewing beer or palm wine.

items.name: Southern Bantu Peoples
items.overview: Our Southern Bantu Peoples region is full of subtropical grasslands and coastlines, where locals have fished in Lake Malawi and the Indian Ocean for generations. Bantu-speaking peoples arrived between the 1st century BCE and the 4th century CE and continued spreading over the next millennium. The region boasts enormous cultural diversity. People practice Islam, Christianity, and Indigenous African religions, and they speak Bantu languages (including Swahili, Chichewa, Shona, Zulu, and Xhosa) along with European languages (including English, Portuguese, and Afrikaans). Much of popular culture in this region is influenced by this convergence of cultures, such as the musical styles of marrabenta and mbaqanga.
items.primaryLocated: Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, South Africa, Zimbabwe
items.alsoLocated: Kenya, Namibia, Madagascar, Seychelles, Tanzania, Zambia

items.name: Khoisan, Aka & Mbuti Peoples
items.overview: Populations in our Khoisan, Aka & Mbuti Peoples region include hunter-gatherer and pastoral groups whose ancestors have lived in Africa for thousands of years. They make their homes in many different climes, from rainforests to savannas, and are known for their intimate knowledge of the landscapes they live in. Though small in number, these peoples are now drawing the attention of scholars and researchers for their genetic diversity, ancient origins, and unique cultural traditions and knowledge that have been passed down for centuries.
items.alsoLocated: Botswana, Central African Republic, Deomcratic Republic of the Congo, Gabon, Republic of the Congo, South Africa, Uganda

items.name: Senegal
items.overview: Africa’s westernmost nation, the namesake of our Senegal region, lies about 1,000 miles above the equator and boasts miles of beaches along the Atlantic. It’s bordered by Mauritania, Mali, Guinea, and Guinea-Bissau and almost completely encircles the Gambia. The country’s current population is just about evenly divided between urban and rural dwellers, with more than 2 million Senegalese now living in and around the capital city of Dakar. Senegal is widely known for its music, including mbalax (“rhythm” in Wolof, the working language of Senegal) and dazzling sabar drumming.
items.alsoLocated: Cape Verde, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Sierra Leone

items.name: Central West Africa
items.overview: From the humid coast of the Gulf of Guinea, our Central West Africa region stretches north into the semi-arid Sahel. For centuries, powerful empires traded here with Arab and Berber (Imazighen) merchants from North Africa. European colonists later brought French, English, and Christianity to an area already replete with a variety of languages and spiritual practices. Despite vast cultural differences, many inhabitants share practices, including their staple diet (a starchy paste made from cassava, millet, or corn and served with sauce and occasionally meat), spiritual veneration of ancestors, locally brewed palm wine, and elaborate celebrations to mark both weddings and funerals.
items.alsoLocated: Central African Republic, Sao Tome & Principe, Sierra Leone

items.name: Eastern Bantu Peoples
items.overview: The East African Plateau and Lake Victoria—the world’s largest lake by area—are central to our Eastern Bantu Peoples region. The fertile land and ample access to waterways allowed the first Bantu-speaking peoples to settle here about 3,000 years ago. They planted root crops, raised cattle, and fished, activities they carry on today. While British colonization spread English and Christianity, Indigenous and syncretic religions endure, as does multilingualism—people speak dozens of languages in this region. These diverse cultures find unity in shared traditions such as newborn naming ceremonies, producing banana-based liquors and beers, and the importance placed on music, dance, and hospitality.
items.alsoLocated: Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo,  Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, Rwanda, Tanzania, Zambia, Zimbabwe

items.name: Sephardic Jews in Northern Africa
items.overview: Our North African Sephardic Jewish region encompasses the descendants of Jews who settled in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Libya after being forced out of Spain and Portugal in the late 15th century. They joined long-established Jewish populations in the region, and both groups influenced each other in the centuries that followed. Sephardic Jews in North Africa played important roles as merchants, artisans, translators, and court advisors under various regimes. Their culture often blended Iberian Jewish tradition with North African influences to produce distinct food and music. In the 20th century, many Sephardic Jews left for countries like France and Israel but they still kept their traditions alive.

items.name: Ethiopia & Eritrea
items.overview: Spanning most of the Horn of Africa, our Ethiopia and Eritrea region has a diverse topography that includes deserts, highlands, valleys, and several hundred miles of coastline along the Red Sea. The ancient kingdom of Aksum ruled this area from the 3rd to 6th centuries, controlling the trade of gold and ivory and becoming one of the first African states to adopt Christianity. Today, Ethiopia and Eritrea are ethnically and linguistically diverse nations known for their hospitality, flavorful cuisine, and pastoral traditions.

items.name: Somalia
items.overview: Our Somalia region, encompassing a swath of the Horn of Africa’s coastline, is composed mainly of hot, arid plains and plateaus. The region has two annual rainy seasons—known as gu and day in Somali—that make agriculture possible. The historic Sultanate of Mogadishu was an important trade center beginning in the 10th century for goods including gold and incense. Today, most Somalis practice Islam blended with a unique mix of indigenous beliefs and are known for their rich oral mythology.

items.name: Yorubaland
items.overview: Our Yorubaland region is centered around Benin and southwestern Nigeria. Tropical and coastal, the area has provided abundant fish and fruit to its inhabitants for centuries. When many fell victim to the transatlantic slave trade, they brought their agricultural skills and elements of their spiritual practices, which became known as voodoo or santería, to the Americas. It’s common nowadays for people to speak a European language (English, French, or a related creole) alongside local languages. Hospitality and respect for elders are key aspects of social interactions, and the region’s rich oral tradition means that storytelling is an art enjoyed by all ages.

items.name: North Africa
items.overview: Our North Africa region includes much of the region referred to as the Maghreb. It's an area of stark contrast, with the hospitable Mediterranean coast to the north and the vast, harsh Sahara to the south. In fact, the majority of the population in this region lives within about 50 miles of the Atlantic or Mediterranean coasts.
items.primaryLocated: Algeria, Libya, Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia, Western Sahara

items.name: Western Bantu Peoples
items.overview: Extending through south-central and southwestern Africa, our Western Bantu Peoples region winds through tropical rainforest, humid savanna, and semi-arid desert. Starting about 3,000 years ago, Bantu-speaking peoples spread from an area around the border of modern-day Cameroon and Nigeria through much of sub-Saharan Africa in one of the greatest migrations in human history. Today the region is home to unrivaled ethnic and linguistic diversity.
items.primaryLocated: Angola, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Namibia, Republic of the Congo
items.alsoLocated: Botswana, Burundi, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Kenya, Madagascar, Malawi, Mauritius, Mozambique, Qatar, Reunion, Rwanda, São Tomé & Príncipe, Seychelles, South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia, Zimbabwe

items.name: Central America
items.overview: Lying directly over a volcanic arc with the Pacific Ocean to the west and the Caribbean Sea to the east, our Indigenous Americas—Central America region has been home to various peoples, including the Maya, Lenca,  Pipil, and Xinca. The fertile valleys of this mountainous area made it possible to grow ample crops, such as maize (corn), which could then be used for trade amongst surrounding autonomous and linguistically diverse city-states. Much like Yucatan, the Mayas  of this region are known for producing beautiful codex-style ceramics decorated with complex glyphs depicting astronomical and natural observations, including illustrations of local wildlife.

items.name: Haiti & Dominican Republic
items.overview: Bisected by five mountain ranges, our Indigenous Haiti and the Dominican Republic region covers the second-largest island of the West Indies and enjoys both the benefits and pitfalls of a continuous tropical climate. Arawak-speaking Indigenous peoples from Central and South America settled in this region early on and eventually coalesced into the Taíno. They then divided the island into five caciquats, or chieftaincies, ruled by caciques. Before the arrival of the Spanish in the late 1400s, the thriving Taíno civilization made significant advances in natural medicine, agriculture, and religious art.

items.name: Puerto Rico
items.overview: The Indigenous Puerto Rico region encompasses the archipelago of Puerto Rico, with its main island and more than 140 islets and cays. The Taíno were the primary inhabitants until the Spanish arrived in the late 1400s; they called the island Borinquen, “Land of the Valiant Lord.” The Spanish conquistadors marveled at the complex Taíno ceremonial dances and oral storytelling traditions. The polytheistic Taíno believe that their gods, known as zemi, controlled elements of the natural world, such as wind and fire.

items.name: Arctic
items.overview: Our Indigenous Arctic region extends from northeast Russia across northern Canada. No more than 20,000 years ago, migrants crossed the Bering Sea via a land bridge. Some settled in the area, while others trekked southward. The Arctic is a harsh landscape, cold, flat, and mostly treeless. Early inhabitants, such as the Inuvialuit (Inuit) mastered hunting seals, polar bears, and otters and fishing for food and clothing. They lived in houses made of sod, timber, and ice blocks, and often traveled across the cold terrain with the help of dog sleds, a practice that continues today.

items.name: Colombia & Venezuela
items.overview: With the Andes Mountains to the west and the Orinoco River Basin to the east, hundreds of groups have called our Indigenous Americas—Colombia and Venezuela region home, including the metalworking and mining Muisca and Tairona peoples. The Wayuu are the most numerous Indigenous group in the region. Known for its fertile Llanos grasslands where maize (corn) is still grown, this area also possesses ample natural resources such as rock salt, emeralds, and precious metals. With its present-day resguardos, or reservation lands, this region continues to be shaped by an active, diverse Indigenous population.

items.name: Panama & Costa Rica
items.overview: Located on the narrow, S-shaped strip of land between Nicaragua to the north and Colombia to the southeast, our Indigenous Americas—Panama & Costa Rica region is tropical and mountainous, boasting some of Central America’s most famed beaches and rainforests. Historically, peoples of the region had contact with the Maya, Mexica (Aztec), and Andean (Inca) civilizations but maintained their own distinct artistic styles, which included carved stone artwork and figurines made from gold, jade, and turquoise. Today, most people identify as mestizo, meaning they claim both European and Indigenous American ancestry. More than a dozen Indigenous languages, from the Chibchan language family, are currently spoken in the region.

items.name: Eastern South America
items.overview: Bordered by the Amazon rainforest to the north, the tropical wetlands of Paraguay and Bolivia to the west, and the pampas of Uruguay and Argentina in the south, our Indigenous Eastern South America region covers a wide swath of the continent. The varied landscape led to distinct interior and coastal cultures, and early inhabitants relied heavily on diverse flora and fauna, even processing potentially toxic plants such as cassava for food or medicine. The Indigenous peoples of this region are part of the Tupi-Guarani language family. The tropical rainforests remain home to several small semi-settled and nomadic groups who isolate themselves from the outside world.

items.name: Bolivia & Peru
items.overview: Our Indigenous Americas—Bolivia & Peru region extends across the Central Andes from the Pacific Ocean to the western edge of the Amazon rainforest. With over 10,000 years of human settlement, this area has been home to a wide variety of groups, including Kichwa (Quechua) and Aymara speakers. Andean cultures practiced diverse agriculture, developed sophisticated highway systems, and made notable medical advances using products from three distinct ecological zones. The Inca capital of Cuzco was at the center of a quadripartite empire. The Incan estate of Machu Picchu is of particular interest due to its mountain views, temples, and man-made rock terraces.
items.alsoLocated: Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Ecuador, Uruguay, Venezuela

items.name: Ecuador
items.overview: Aptly named for its position straddling the equator, our Indigenous Americas—Ecuador region in northwestern South America is naturally divided by the Andes into the Costa (costal), Sierra (highland), and Oriente (eastern) regions, although the majority of the population resides in the first two. The area was occupied by the Inca Empire during parts of the 15th and 16th centuries and later by Spain. Many Indigenous peoples in Ecuador speak Kichwa (Quechua) and other Indigenous languages. Natives in the region exchanged items from three distinct ecological zones. Today, Ecuadorian culture is celebrated via musical styles including the pasillo, yumbo, and sanjuanito; cuisine such as fanesca, a squash and bean soup eaten at Easter; and the country’s famed pottery and flower markets.

items.name: Canada & United States
items.overview: The diverse landscape of our Indigenous Americas—Canada & United States region spans from the Pacific Canadian Coast to the northern Atlantic coastline. These lands were home to a vast array of Native American groups, from the nomadic tribes of the Plains to more sedentary peoples in the Northeast. Surviving by hunting, foraging, and agriculture, they also traded and formed relationships with French, Spanish, and English travelers. Oral storytelling traditions helped to sustain origin myths, such as the tale of the Iroquoian Sky People, while changing to accommodate new Christian influences. While different in many ways, the people of this region all created societies rich in cultural adaptation.

items.name: Mexico
items.overview: Our Indigenous Americas—Mexico region extends from the southwestern United States down to the border of Guatemala. Known for their large urban city-states, mathematical expertise, and intricate calendars, the advanced culture of the Mexica (Aztecs) called this area home and built their capital where Mexico City now stands. In the northern part of the region, sedentary groups such as the ancestors of the Hopi or the Zuñi became expert farmers and grew squash, corn, and beans in their desert environment. Despite their harsh surroundings, the Indigenous peoples of this region created a rich legacy of art, empire, science, and trade.

items.name: Chile
items.overview: Extending approximately 2,700 miles from the Atacama Desert in the north to its southern tip, this region comprises a narrow, jagged coastline on the western side of the Andes mountains. The area has been populated for at least the last 5,000 years. The Indigenous Araucanians are celebrated to this day for their prolonged resistance to European colonization. Chile became a Spanish colony in the 16th century, but the Araucanians or Mapuche were never entirely subdued. Most Chileans have both European and Indigenous ancestry, visible in cultural expressions including the annual Festival of La Tirana and the national dance, the cueca, which combine elements from both continents.

items.name: Cuba
items.overview: Characterized by hilly terrain and fertile plains, the narrow, arching island at the center of our Indigenous Cuba region was home to various Indigenous peoples, starting with the nomadic gatherer-hunter Ciboney and transitioning to the Taíno by 500 A.D. Adept farmers, the Taíno created settlements on the western part of the island and grew yuca, maize (corn), and beans. The arrival of the Spanish in the late 1400s spelled doom for the natives, who perished through enslavement, disease, and starvation. However, present-day Cubans claim that the Taíno heritage lives on through family links and traditional practices.

items.name: Yucatán Peninsula
items.overview: Our  Indigenous Americas—Yucatán Peninsula region lies between the Gulf of Mexico to the west and north and the Caribbean Sea to the east. The collection of Indigenous peoples known as the Maya established agricultural settlements in this region as early as 1500 B.C. They planted maize (corn), squash, and beans for daily consumption and built striking city-states, such as Uxmal, Chichen Itzá, and many more which still stand today. Maya society was incredibly stratified, with nobles, commoners, and enslaved people. They also used a glyphic writing system and are known for their architecture, astronomy, monumental art, and complicated cyclical calendrical system.

items.name: Gulf of Khambhat
items.overview: The Gulf of Khambhat, where India’s powerful Narmada River and many smaller waterways flow into the Arabian Sea, is a watery region of sand flats, shoals, and wetlands. But its important ports, like Bharuch and Surat, have long been important entry points for commerce, sending Indian goods and capital to the world and vice versa. Diamonds, textiles, and spices were and remain important exports from the region to the world. A well-developed vegetarian cuisine—typified by undhiyu, a slow-cooked vegetable dish with green beans, banana, and eggplant—speaks to the enduring influence of Jain culture in the region.

items.name: Northern & Central Philippines
items.overview: Among thousands of islands in the Philippines archipelago, the populations in our Northern & Central Philippines region are centered around the central & southern half of the Luzon island group, home to the capital city of Manila. The diverse people who have occupied these islands for over a millennium practiced different religions and spoke different languages, but 350 years of Spanish occupation, and nearly half a century of American colonization, worked to centralize Filipino government and culture. Today, most Filipinos practice Roman Catholicism, and Spanish place names are common throughout the islands, but many elements of modern daily life predate European arrival, including the Tagalog language and administrative divisions known as barangays.

items.name: Lower Central Asia
items.overview: Our Lower Central Asia region encompasses Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and parts of Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and Kyrgyzstan. The mountainous terrain makes human settlement difficult in many places, but the oases, foothills, and the fertile Fergana Valley boast larger populations. The famed Silk Road connected this region to eastern China and western Europe for over a millennium, and Islam, introduced around the 8th century, was widely practiced. The region was heavily influenced during Soviet rule, with an increase in factories and state-owned farms, bans on religious education, and censorship of media. Since independence, many have reclaimed elements of their cultural heritage, including the practice of Islam.

items.name: Japan
items.overview: Our Japan population region includes the four largest Japanese islands, stretching from the southern tip of Kyushu to northern Hokkaido. The islands’ temperate climate brings four distinct seasons to most parts of Japan, as well as abundant summer rain known as baiu (“plum rain”) because it coincides with the start of plum season. Japanese administrators adopted and then adapted many elements from China’s Tang Dynasty, including its writing system, and in turn built a nation that exerted influence across the world. Modern-day Japan is a world leader in finance and technology, and its art, cuisine, and design have gained global fame.

items.name: Central & Southern Philippines
items.overview: The people of our Central & Southern Philippines region call much of the Visayan island group and Mindanao, the second-largest island in the Philippines archipelago, home. Known for their tropical climate, long coastline, and numerous lakes and rivers, these islands are ideal for fishing and growing abacá, or Manila hemp, a fibrous plant used to make twine and rope. Filipino farmers grew this crop for centuries before it gained the attention of Spanish and American colonists. Filipino culture today is a blend of Eastern, Western, and local traditions and influences, which can be seen in holidays such as the Sinulog Festival, a Catholic celebration that also commemorates local religious practices.

items.name: Iran/Persia
items.overview: Mountains are the defining feature of our Iran/Persia region’s landscape, from the Greater Caucasus in Azerbaijan to the Kopet Dag range along the border of Iran and Turkmenistan. High plateaus and deserts are also common the further east you go. It’s the land of the ancient Persian Empire, once ruled by Cyrus the Great, and still home to a variety of languages, literature, and cultures that have proved more lasting than any kingdom.
items.alsoLocated: Afghanistan, Bahrain, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Qatar, Tajikistan, Turkey, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan

items.name: Luzon
items.overview: Of the Philippines’ 2,000 inhabited islands, our Luzon region centers around its largest and most populous island. Named for King Philip II of Spain, Filipino culture was strongly impacted by over 300 years of Spanish rule. After independence from Spain in 1898, United States occupation lasted nearly 50 years. The influence of Western culture can be seen in colonial-era Spanish cathedrals, Spanish loanwords in the Filipino language, the popularity of basketball and American media, and an education system based on U.S. influence. Cultural elements that fuse Asian culture with Western culture include formal men’s shirts called barongs, and banana ketchup, common in fast food restaurants.

items.name: Burusho
items.overview: Our Burusho region is named for a people who live in the high Hunza, Nagar, and Yasin Valleys in the Gilgit-Baltistan territory of northern Pakistan. Their villages lie at elevations of 9,000 feet, surrounded by the ice fields and towering peaks of the Karakoram Mountains. They lived a fairly isolated life until the Karakoram Highway connected Pakistan and China in 1978.

items.name: Tibetan Peoples
items.overview: The towering Tibetan Plateau lies at the heart of our Tibetan Peoples region. The region’s staggering elevation—over 13,000 feet above sea level in most areas—has earned it the nickname “the roof of the world.” The region’s isolated location allowed a unique culture to develop, including the Tibetan writing system and Tibetan Buddhism. Most people are subsistence farmers who consume staples such as barley and yak meat. Local and national festivals are based on the Tibetan calendar and often include feasts, music, and dancing.

items.name: Bengal
items.overview: In the Ganges Delta that forms the majority of our Bengal region—which includes Bangladesh and parts of India, as well as Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar and western China—rivers and other waterways shape inhabitants’ way of life. Agriculture, fishing, and the monsoon season are of central importance. Centuries of Buddhist, Hindu, and Muslim rule in the region’s early history created a pluralistic society; today, most in Bangladesh practice Islam while the Bengalis of India practice Islam and Hinduism. One of the most defining features of Bengali identity, however, remains the Bangla language, spoken in Bangladesh and India and ranking fifth in the world in terms of the number of native speakers.

items.name: Anatolia & the Caucasus
items.overview: In our Anatolia and the Caucasus region, the Anatolian Plateau stretches to the west, rugged, mountainous country that slopes down to the shores of the Aegean Sea. To the east are the Armenian Highlands, the birthplace of ironworking—and some say the Garden of Eden. As a physical bridge between Europe and Asia, this region has seen empires—Greeks, Persians, Romans, Ottomans—come and go for thousands of years.

items.name: Southwestern China
items.overview: Our Southwestern China region covers the Chinese provinces of Sichuan, Yunnan, Guizhou, and the megalopolis of Chongqing. This mountainous region is bisected by the Yangtze River, the longest river in Asia and a feature that has profoundly shaped China’s culture and economy, both past and present. Ancient civilizations began cultivating tea in Yunnan over 4,000 years ago, and in time, tea helped make China a center for international trade. Today, the region is known for the spicy food of its Sichuan provinces and the more delicate fare of Yunnan cuisine, as well as for its ethnic and cultural diversity.

items.name: Dai
items.overview: Most modern-day inhabitants in our Dai region live in or around China’s Yunnan Province, on the boundary where China meets Southeast Asia both geographically and culturally. However, people have made their homes in the mountains and river valleys, including the floodplains of the Mekong, for thousands of years. They were among the first in Asia to use oxen to plow. Artifacts from the Greek and Roman Empires show longstanding trade between east and west, and they were influenced by both Indian and Chinese culture.
items.alsoLocated: Lao People's Democratic Republic, Thailand, Vietnam

items.name: Indo-Gangetic Plain
items.overview: The “Hindi Heartland” of Northern India is one of the world’s most fertile regions: the volcanic ash which once washed down from the Himalayas has supported one of the world’s largest populations for millennia. The historical homeland of one of the world’s major religions, Buddhism, was also a central region for the development of early Hinduism, and grounds for a rich Islamic culture from the 13th century onwards. That shared legacy is evident everywhere from the Indo-Islamic architecture of the Taj Mahal, the ghats of Varanasi on the Ganges River, and the Buddhist pilgrimage sites around Bodh Gaya.

items.name: Southern Japanese Islands
items.overview: Our Southern Japanese Islands population region includes the Ryukyu or Nansei Islands, a tropical and subtropical archipelago that extends from Japan to Taiwan. For nearly 300 years, these islands constituted the Ryukyu Kingdom, where traditional crafts developed, including distinctive pottery and textile production. Although the Ryukyus were incorporated into Japan in the late 19th century and struggled to maintain their culture in the face of a Meiji-era effort to suppress it, they have retained their unique identity. The islanders continue to speak distinct variants of Japanese and celebrate holidays unknown on the mainland.

items.name: Southern India
items.overview: Southern India includes the modern Indian states of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and parts of Karnataka. The region’s coastal planes slope up gently towards the rainy Nilgiri hills. Criss-crossed by the Kaveri and Godavari rivers, Southern India produces rice, lentils, and a range of spices, and its cuisine ranges from vegetarian staples like idli and sambar to rich Hyderabadi biryani. India’s classical arts like Bharatanatyam dance and Carnatic music have long flourished here, and important archeological sites like Hampi speak to the region’s historical wealth and power, which once radiated across the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal.
items.alsoLocated: Pakistan, Maldives, Mauritius, Seychelles, South Africa, Sri Lanka

items.name: Southwest India
items.overview: Irrigated by the summer monsoon, which arrives from the Arabian Sea, Southwest India is bounded in the east by the Western Ghats, a low-lying mountain range which keeps the region perennially lush and green. The coastal region’s celebrated cuisine is based largely on coconut and fish—still occasionally caught in large, Chinese-style nets—and further up the ghats, coffee and tea are important cash crops for export. An important region for the practice of Ayurveda—one of India’s traditional medical systems—Southwest India is also known for the folk dances of Theyyam and Kathakali.

items.name: Northern Iraq & Northern Iran
items.overview: The mountainous highlands that make up our Northern Iraq and Northern Iran region have been home to renowned civilizations, including Assyria, Babylonia, and later the Persian, Greek, and Roman empires. Today, most inhabitants are adherents of Shia Islam, although Sunni Islam has many practitioners as well. The region’s ancient architecture includes remnants of pre-Islamic dynasties as well as Arabic, Ottoman, and Persian constructions. The most widely-spoken languages are Arabic, Farsi, and Kurdish. Typical cuisine includes lamb seasoned with lemon and garlic, yogurts and cheeses, fresh fruits and vegetables, and black tea and coffee.

items.name: Levant
items.overview: Our Levant region radiates outward from Lebanon to include Syria, Jordan, Israel, and the Palestinian territories along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean Sea. Home to the ancient city of Petra and the Phoenician port city of Byblos, the region’s maritime position made it an important center of trade throughout antiquity. Today, it remains a cultural crossroads where Arabic, Hebrew, French, and English are widely spoken and elements of European, Arab, and Mediterranean cultures merge. The region shares the values of family and kinship, and cuisine that includes olives, grilled meat, and sweets baked with pistachios, almonds, or honey.
items.primaryLocated: Israel/Palestine, Jordan, Lebanon, Syrian Arab Republic

items.name: Korea
items.overview: Geography has helped shape the people of our Korea region’s identity. The east and north are mountainous, while plains in the south and west provide farmland. Living on a peninsula gave Koreans access to ideas and goods from both continental and maritime contacts. The roots of modern Korea began during the Three Kingdoms Period (220-280 A.D.), and Korea has unique and ancient traditions of pottery, art, and dance. After the devastation of WWII and the Korean War, Koreans rebuilt their country into an industrial and technical powerhouse, and cultural exports like Korean cuisine, cinema, and “K-pop” are becoming mainstream in countries the world over.

items.name: Western Visayas
items.overview: Our Western Visayas region encompasses many of the islands in the central Philippines, situated south of Luzon and just north of Mindanao. Through centuries of trade, over 300 years of Spanish colonization, and nearly 50 years of United States occupation, many parts of the Western Visayas have retained a distinct cultural identity. While Roman Catholicism is practiced by most inhabitants, animist religions are still found in some rural areas. Rice farming is one of the most common occupations, and rice serves as the basis of nearly every meal. Filipinos have a rich tradition of myths and legends, shaped by contact with Hinduism, Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism.

items.name: Mainland Southeast Asia
items.overview: Our Mainland Southeast Asia region is centered in Cambodia, extends over Thailand, Laos, and Myanmar. From upland forests and river deltas to rugged coasts and tropical islands, the geography of Mainland Southeast Asia is as diverse as its people, who collectively speak several hundred languages. Inhabitants of this region have been in contact with each other for millennia and have participated in both overland and maritime trading with China, India, and Europe. Despite notable exceptions such as Bangkok, this region is “a land of villages”: most of its inhabitants live in rural areas, where fishing and rice farming are central to many people’s daily lives.

items.name: Western China
items.overview: Our Western China region—which extends from the Chinese provinces of Xinjiang, Qinghai, and Gansu to Myanmar, Bhutan, and Tibet in the south—covers some of China’s largest but most sparsely populated regions. Although most of the region falls geopolitically within Chinese borders, it is divided culturally from the Mandarin-speaking Han majority in the eastern coastal metropolises. The Taklamakan Desert, the Gobi Desert, and the Himalayan mountains have made it difficult to practice agriculture in this area, but a number of China’s largest minority groups—including Tibetans, Uyghurs, and Kazakhs—have made it their home for centuries. They have retained their own languages, cultural practices, and religions. Their social and geographic separation from majority Chinese culture has allowed them to maintain their distinct cultural identities.

items.name: The Deccan & the Gulf of Mannar
items.overview: This vast region spans the width of southern India and extends across the island of Sri Lanka. Its diverse populations, largely speakers of Dravidian languages, have long produced a culture distinct from their northern Indian counterparts, even as they have remained connected to the wider world through extensive global trade networks. These populations have made their mark in architecture, from the Ajanta and Ellora caves in the region’s north to the Meenakshi Amman Temple in its south, and cuisine, from fiery, fish-based coastal cuisines to the vegetarian feasts of certain southern communities.
items.alsoLocated: Bangladesh, Mauritius, Reunion, Seychelles, South Africa

items.name: Central & Eastern China & Taiwan
items.overview: Our Central & Eastern China & Taiwan region extends from the mountains of Hubei and Hunan Provinces in the west to cosmopolitan Shanghai and down to Taiwan in the east. The foothills, fertile lowlands, and subtropical climate have made it home to civilization for millennia. This long history has produced a rich variety of cultural expressions seen in local art, including forms of opera, as well as cuisine—the region boasts five of China’s “Eight Major Cuisines”: Hunan, Fujian, Zhejiang, Anhui, and Jiangsu. Today, Shanghai and Taipei are the cultural, industrial, and technological capitals of the area.

items.name: Nepal & the Himalayan Foothills
items.overview: Our Nepal and the Himalayan Foothills region slopes from the southern and eastern ridges of the Himalayas into the fertile valleys below. The Himalayas have long been linked with the area’s two major religions, Hinduism and Buddhism: the Hindu gods are said to reside here, and Nepal is held to be the birthplace of the Buddha. Despite bordering two economic superpowers—China and India—the area has remained largely rural. Many people farm and live in villages or market towns, where hospitality and etiquette are central aspects of local culture.

items.name: Maritime Southeast Asia
items.overview: Our Maritime Southeast Asia region, which comprises several thousand islands and miles of coastline, includes the coastal nations of Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Brunei, Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste, and the Aboriginal peoples of Australia. Some of these islands were inhabited by early humans beginning over 1.5 million years ago, and for the past several thousand years, they have connected cultures along maritime trade routes between mainland Asia and Oceania. Although the majority of the region’s inhabitants are rural, the widespread practice of Islam and Christianity point to a long history of influence from overseas cultures. Today, the highly urbanized and dense metropolises of Kuala Lumpur, Singapore, and Jakarta serve as the region’s economic and cultural hubs and are home to highly diverse populations.

items.name: Mongolia & Upper Central Asia
items.overview: Climate and terrain has shaped the history and people of our Mongolia and Upper Central Asia region, which includes temperate grasslands, arid deserts, and rugged mountains. Kazakhstan can be translated as “land of wanderers,” and a nomadic, pastoral lifestyle has dominated this region since the Stone Age. Horses were probably domesticated on the vast Eurasian steppes, and for centuries fearsome warriors on horseback, including Genghis Khan, founded empires that at one point stretched from the Pacific Ocean to the Black Sea.

items.name: Vietnam
items.overview: The peninsula at the center of our Vietnam region is home to peoples who trace their ancestry back to the time of myth. Rivers, such as the famous Mekong, run between mountain ranges and often end in large lowland deltas, and the climate is shaped by monsoons that bring wet and dry seasons as the prevailing winds change directions. The cooperation required to build the dams, dikes, and canals vital to farming led people to form states and develop societies that borrowed from both Indian and Chinese cultures while maintaining languages, identities, and customs that set them apart.

items.name: Northern China
items.overview: From the Taklamakan and Gobi Deserts in the west to the bustling capital city of Beijing in the east, our Northern Chinese population region encompasses a large portion of China’s ethnic diversity, which includes Han Chinese, Uyghur, and Tibetan peoples. China’s written history dates back several millennia, which has allowed its extensive contributions to philosophy, technology, music, and cooking to be well preserved. Beijing is the cultural and political center of Northern China and the nation generally. The city is famed for its Jing cuisine, its abundant teahouses, and jingxi, or local opera.

items.name: Southern China
items.overview: Our Southern China region reaches from mountainous Guangxi to bustling Hong Kong and the southern coastline along the South China Sea. Geography kept the population separated from the rest of China for centuries, but maritime trade routes led to contact with Europe and the Arab world. Present-day Southern China has maintained much of its unique character and is home to some of China’s largest ethnic minority populations, especially the Zhuang. Cantonese language and culture, including Cantonese opera and cuisine, have spread far beyond southern China. War, poverty, and proximity to the ocean also made the region the largest source of Chinese emigrants in the 19th and 20th centuries.

items.name: Western Himalayas & the Hindu Kush
items.overview: The plains of Punjab and Haryana lie far below the formidable peaks of the Himalayas, the world’s highest mountain range, and are irrigated by the rushing Indus River. The mountainous region’s diverse ecologies span present-day India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, and are home to an impressively diverse range of cultures, from Buddhist Ladakh to Muslim-majority Kashmir. In the former, Buddhist monasteries dot a craggy landscape, and in the latter, 20th-century conflict has not diminished the strength of a distinctly regional culture, characterized by distinct cuisine and a particularly celebrated world of textiles and handicrafts.
items.alsoLocated: China, India, Iran, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan

items.name: Gujarat
items.overview: If many know Gujarat as the birthplace of Mohandas Gandhi, it remains one of the Indian subcontinent’s most culturally and materially wealthy and diverse regions, with a landscape that spans from its extensive coastline to its lush forests and wide white salt flats. Largely vegetarian, and renowned for dishes like dhokla and khandvi, Gujarat has long been linked to the world by extensive trade along its long coastline. Its energetic and colorful craftwork has led to distinctly regional textiles, from Patola silk weaving to Bandhani tie-dyes.

items.name: Arabian Peninsula
items.overview: Our Arabian Peninsula region is centered in Yemen and Saudi Arabia. Beyond the peninsula’s cities, land is mostly inhospitable desert with the exception of oases that are dotted with date palm groves and wadis, valleys that turn into riverbeds during periods of heavy rain. The area served to control trade among ancient Egypt, India, and Rome, and it was the 6th-century birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad in Mecca, which sparked the advent of Islam. Today, the oil industry has increased urbanization, but traditional values including kinship, hospitality, and generosity are still observed.
items.alsoLocated: Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Libya, Oman, Palestine, Qatar, Sudan

items.name: Northern Asia
items.overview: Our Northern Asia region reaches from the steppes of Central Asia into the mountains and rivers of Siberia and Russia’s far east. Many of the region’s inhabitants today, such as the Daur, Hezhen, and Xibo, share a historical connection to the Khitan Empire, which once stretched from Mongolia to northern Korea. Many were nomadic or semi-nomadic peoples who have resettled a number of times before reaching the lands they occupy today.

items.name: East Midlands
items.overview: The East Midlands sits at the heart of England. It stretches from the industrial cities of Nottingham and Leicester to the rolling countryside of Lincolnshire. During Britain's Industrial Revolution, Nottingham’s coal miners worked deep underground while factories made everything from textiles to machines. This industrial landscape developed not far from the ancient oaks of Sherwood Forest, legendary home of Robin Hood. Eastward, Lincolnshire’s farmlands became known as England's vegetable garden, supporting crops like potatoes, sugar beets, and peas. The East Midlands’ cities, historic countryside, and fertile land have created a unique character of both industry and natural beauty.

items.name: Sicily
items.overview: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean Sea, located between Europe and Africa. The Phoenicians, Greeks, Romans, Arabs, Normans, and Spanish all left their mark on the island's culture. Sicily’s architectural heritage ranges from Greek temples to Baroque churches. Local cuisine features fresh seafood and citrus, blending Arab and Italian influences in dishes like arancini (fried rice balls) and caponata (a vegetable dish). Golden beaches, rocky sulfur mines, rolling farmland, and Mount Etna are all part of the landscape that has helped shape a people known for their warmth, storytelling traditions, and deep connection to the land and sea.

items.name: Brittany, France
items.overview: Our Brittany region, located in northwest France, has deep Celtic roots. Once an independent duchy with ties to Wales and Cornwall, Brittany retains its own language, Breton—a Celtic language related to Welsh. The landscape is dotted with prehistoric stone monuments, medieval chapels, and fortified coastal towns. Local folklore includes legends of korrigans (small, mischievous spirits), enchanted forests like Paimpoint, and the sunken city of Ys (pronounced “ees”), said to lie beneath the sea. Brittany’s maritime heritage continues to shape daily life, with fishing ports and salt marshes, and its culinary specialties—including seafood, crêpes, galettes, cider, and rich, buttery pastries called kouign-amann—reflecting both Celtic and French influences.

items.name: Northern Wales & North West England
items.overview: Our Northern Wales and North West England region stretches from the Welsh mountains of Snowdonia to the busy English cities of Manchester and Liverpool. The region includes the beautiful Lake District, rugged coastlines, and Cheshire’s rolling hills. North West England was a powerhouse of the Industrial Revolution. Manchester became known as "Cottonopolis" because of its many textile mills, and Liverpool grew into a critical port, with docks handling much of the imported cotton that fueled Britain's textile industry. North Wales is known for its distinctive language, ancient castles, and mountain scenery. This region combines industrial heritage with some of Britain's most beautiful natural landscapes.

items.name: Donegal, Ireland
items.overview: Our Donegal region lies in the northwest corner of Ireland, in the province of Ulster. It is part of the Republic of Ireland. Known for its high cliffs, rugged mountains, and ancient castles, it is geographically isolated. It is only connected to the rest of Ireland by a small border with County Leitrim. People have lived there since prehistoric times, leaving behind stone circles and ringforts. Medieval monastic ruins are evidence of the later arrival of Christianity. Donegal has a strong Gaelic culture. The Irish name for County Donegal, Dún na nGall means “fort of the foreigners,” a nod to early Viking or seafaring contact. Traditional music, dancing, and storytelling are still part of everyday life.

items.name: France
items.overview: Our France region stretches from the English Channel and its northern border to its southern coast along the Mediterranean Sea, and includes a diversity of landscapes, from the Atlantic coast and Mediterranean shores to the Alps, Pyrenees, and central plains. The region has been shaped by Celtic, Roman, Germanic, and Mediterranean peoples over many centuries. While French is the official national language today, several regional languages are still spoken. France is also home to a rich architectural heritage, from Roman amphitheaters and medieval cathedrals to Renaissance castles and modern cityscapes. Food and wine, including Provençal vegetables, delicate pastries, Alpine cheeses, and Burgundy wines, are central to daily life.

items.name: Finland
items.overview: Finland is one of the Nordic nations straddling the Arctic Circle north of continental Europe. Although it shares long borders with the Scandinavian nations of Sweden and Norway, our Finland region stands apart in both language and ethnic identity. Politically controlled by its neighbors Sweden and Russia through much of its history, Finland (Suomi) today is a strong, independent nation with a unique, ancient heritage.

items.name: Russia
items.overview: Spanning over 6.5 million square miles, our Russia region is a land of epic proportions—not only due to its vast size but also because of the impact of its history, politics, and culture on the world. Most of the population lives in Western Russia, in and around the cities of Moscow and Saint Petersburg. Large swaths of the country remain uninhabited or sparsely populated due to the inhospitable climate. Some quintessentially Russian activities include celebrating Maslyanitsa, the Russian holiday that marks the end of winter; marking special occasions with vodka accompanied by zakuski (a spread of snacks); and drinking tea from a samovar, Russia’s traditional metal tea kettle.

items.name: Western Balkans
items.overview: The Western Balkans region, situated in Southeastern Europe, encompasses a variety of landscapes—from rugged mountains and river valleys to its Adriatic coastline. With centuries of Ottoman, Austro-Hungarian, and Slavic influence, the region is known for its vibrant mix of cultures and languages. Major religions in the region include Orthodox Christianity, Islam, and Catholicism. Many families hold tightly to cultural traditions that have been passed down for generations, and the folk dances, handmade textiles, and café culture of the Western Balkans are highly valued.
items.alsoLocated: Bulgaria, Croatia, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia

items.name: Southeastern England & Northwestern Europe
items.overview: The regions along the English Channel share more than a thousand years of history. Southern England, French Normandy, and the Low Countries of Belgium and the Netherlands have been linked by trade, conquest, and cultural exchange since medieval times. Imported Cotswold wool was spun by Flemish weavers, Norman stones and architectural styles shaped English cathedrals. Such commercial connections preceded William the Conqueror's 1066 invasion, which transformed English history and language. Centuries later, these coastlines became battlegrounds during the World Wars of the 1900s. Today, the Channel Tunnel, shipping routes, and airlines continue the connection, linking England and mainland Europe.

items.name: Spain
items.overview: The heart of our Spain region lies in the Iberian Peninsula, framed by the granite peaks and plunging falls of the Pyrenees on the French border in the north and sunny Mediterranean beaches in the south. Waves of invaders throughout history, including Celts and Romans, have fought to establish a presence in this region with varying degrees of success. Muslim rule brought advances in science and education, while the Age of Exploration funneled the world’s wealth into Spain’s coffers. Considering the colonial influence of this region, it is unsurprising that Spanish remains the second-most spoken native language to this day.

items.name: West Midlands
items.overview: Known as “the workshop of the world,” the West Midlands helped develop transportation systems that expanded Britain’s economic power. During the Industrial Revolution, Birmingham’s jewelry quarter produced fine metalwork. Nearby iron and steel production covered the Black Country with coal dust and smoke, leaving residents with persistent breathing problems. Today, the region is the center of Britain's car industry, home to companies like Jaguar and Land Rover. Birmingham offers a vibrant food scene and music venues within driving distance of the peaceful countryside of Shropshire and Warwickshire. The region remains an important center for manufacturing, technology, and transportation in modern England.

items.name: Aegean Islands
items.overview: The Aegean Islands are a group of volcanic islands located in the Aegean Sea between mainland Greece and Turkey. They include islands like Rhodes, Mykonos, and Lesbos. The islands have a rugged, rocky landscape with beautiful beaches and clear blue waters. In ancient times, the Aegean Islands were important for trade and culture, home to civilizations like the Minoans and Mycenaeans. Today, many islanders still fish, farm olives, and welcome tourists. Several of the islands have a rich wine-making tradition. The Aegean Islands are also known for their whitewashed houses, traditional music, and lively festivals.

items.name: Southwestern Balkans
items.overview: Rugged mountain ranges, ancient trade routes, and coastal towns characterize our Southwestern Balkans region. Its history includes Illyrian tribes, as well as the Byzantine and Ottoman empires. The region’s cultural fabric is a blend of Orthodox Christian, Muslim, and Catholic traditions. Hospitality is central to social life, and regional dishes include grilled meats and savory pies. Music, storytelling, and folk dancing remain key forms of expression. Despite changing borders and political shifts, many families maintain strong regional pride and deep ties to ancestral customs.
items.alsoLocated: Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Greece, Romania, Serbia

items.name: Western Ukraine
items.overview: Our Western Ukraine region is a land of natural wonders, UNESCO World Heritage sites, and cities such as Lviv, Uzhhorod, and Chernivtsi. It includes the Carpathian Mountains, with their lakes and forests, and the fertile Dniester River basin. Many people in Western Ukraine speak both Ukrainian and local dialects. Close cultural ties link the region with neighbors Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, and Moldova. The region is known for intricate handicrafts such as embroidered shirts and painted Easter eggs. Unfortunately, Russian aggression has threatened even this westernmost region of Ukraine, but the local culture remains strong.

items.name: Canary Islands
items.overview: The Canary Islands, a Spanish archipelago of volcanic origin, lie off the coast of northwest Africa. With over 2,000 years of human settlement, the area has been home to a number of Indigenous peoples, often referred to collectively as Guanches. With a year-round mild climate and lush vegetation, the islands have a reputation for delicious cuisine, often featuring sancocho fish stew and fresh tropical fruits. From lounging on beaches to kitesurfing, the Canaries offer an array of outdoor adventures for locals and tourists alike. More recently, fueled by an ongoing diaspora, Canarian communities now exist across the globe from Venezuela to Puerto Rico, spreading island culture and values.

items.name: Southern Italy
items.overview: Southern Italy's history has been shaped by its rugged environment and foreign rule. Greeks began colonizing the region in the 8th century BC, planting olive groves that still produce oil today. Byzantine emperors controlled much of Puglia and Calabria, leaving behind painted churches and fortress towns. Norman knights built stone castles to defend the countryside. Spanish kings charged heavy taxes, and peasants got creative with simple meals from ingredients like tomatoes, garlic, and herbs. Frequent earthquakes taught people to rebuild quickly. This harsh existence shaped a culture where survival depended on family and neighbors, simplicity, and determination.

items.name: Northwestern Balkans
items.overview: Mountain peaks, forested hills, and a rugged coastline define the geography of the Northwestern Balkans. Historically influenced by the Roman, Venetian, and Habsburg empires, this area developed a unique blend of Central European and Mediterranean cultures. Roman Catholicism is prominent, and traditional music, lace-making, and regional cuisine—such as seafood stews and hearty breads—play a significant role in family gatherings. While urban centers have grown, many traditions remain rooted in rural customs and close-knit community life.
items.alsoLocated: Bulgaria, Greece, Hungary, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania, Slovenia

items.name: Albania
items.overview: Albania, situated along the Adriatic and Ionian seas, is marked by rugged mountains, ancient ruins, and a coastline rich in history. Its people trace their origins to the ancient Illyrians, and the country has absorbed influences from Greek, Roman, Byzantine, and Ottoman cultures over the centuries. Albania’s culture is deeply rooted in hospitality, music, and strong family bonds. Besa, a deeply rooted concept of honor in Albania, signifies a commitment to keep one’s word and protect the people under one’s care, especially guests. Polyphonic singing and strong kinship networks enrich community life.
items.alsoLocated: Bulgaria, Greece, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania

items.name: Denmark
items.overview: Our Denmark region occupies the Jutland peninsula and over 400 nearby islands that make up the nation. Culturally and geographically, Denmark is part of Scandinavia, and many elements of its history, language, and culture overlap with those of Norway and Sweden. Early Scandinavian culture was spread between the 8th and 11th centuries by Vikings, who raided and settled various parts of Europe. Today, Denmark’s constitutional monarchy is the oldest kingdom in Europe, dating back to at least the 9th century. Despite its small size, Denmark has made substantial contributions to the arts, humanities, and sciences.
items.alsoLocated: Belgium, England, Faroe Islands, the Netherlands

items.name: Eastern European Roma
items.overview:
The early Romani people left northern India in the 9th or 10th centuries and arrived in Europe some 400 years later. Many preserved their nomadic lifestyle, in part because of Europe’s distrust of outsiders and economic competition, since Romani men were recognized for being skilled livestock traders, metalworkers, woodworkers, and basket-weavers. Throughout the Middle Ages and into modern history, discrimination and legal persecution targeting the Romani persisted, and hundreds of thousands were killed in the Porajmos—the genocide of Romani people in Nazi concentration camps. Today, along with the Romani language, other symbols of Romani pride and identity are on the rise, including radio programs, magazines, and the adoption of the Romani flag in 1971.

 

Please note that your ethnicity results do not prove or disprove that you belong to a particular ethnic group. Identifying with, or being a member of, an ethnic or cultural group involves much more than genetics.
items.alsoLocated: Albania, Bosnia and Herzogovia, Croatia, Czechia Republic, Hungary, Kosovo, Moldova, Montenegro, Slovakia, Spain, Turkey

items.name: Slovakia
items.overview: Our Slovakia region is centered on the eastern half of the country, with its deep connections to western Slovakia, eastern Hungary, southern Poland, and western Ukraine. This mountainous and forested region has seen a blending of cultures from ancient migrations through centuries of foreign rule and influence under the Austrians, Hungarians, Nazis, and Soviet Communists. Slovakian independence in 1993 led to a flowering of Slovak culture in museums and regional folk festivals. Locals and visitors alike enjoy the historic city of Košice, the wooden homes and churches of the Carpathian highlanders, and abundant hiking, skiing, and caving.

items.name: Northwestern Italy
items.overview: Stretching from the snowy Alps to the warm Mediterranean coast, Northwestern Italy has long been a place of innovation. The rich farmland of the Po River Valley and the busy ports along the Ligurian coast gave people the resources and reasons to make world-changing achievements. The region fostered Renaissance artists like Leonardo da Vinci, merchants who started Europe's first banks, and designers who made Milan a center of global fashion. Today, this tradition of excellence continues with world-famous Barolo wines, plus modern designers, artists, and inventors who still attract visitors and business leaders from around the world.

items.name: Cornwall
items.overview: Our Cornwall region in England is known for its dramatic cliffs and windswept maritime landscapes. Jutting out into the Atlantic Ocean, its remote seaside location made it a center for maritime trade, fishing, and tin mining. Its relative isolation from the rest of England has also given it a distinctive cultural heritage, influenced by the ancient Celts and prehistoric peoples who erected stone megaliths that are still standing today. Celtic influence can also be seen in the local language, Cornish, which is related to Welsh and Breton. Cornwall’s rich folklore includes tales of mermaids, giants, fairies, gnomes, and, of course, the legendary King Arthur. Cornish cuisine includes clotted cream, commonly served on English scones and savory meat-filled pastries known as pasties.

items.name: Sardinia
items.overview: Sardinia is the second-largest island in the Mediterranean after Sicily. Its craggy mountains pushed up from the ocean in the Paleozoic era more than 250 million years ago. Rome, Spain, and Italy have all left their mark on Sardinian history, but even in the face of outside influences, the island has developed and maintained a culture, language, and cuisine of its own.

items.name: Leinster, Ireland
items.overview: Bordered by the Irish Sea and home to the famed rolling hills of Ireland’s landscapes, our Leinster region covers Ireland’s eastern provinces, including the capital city, Dublin. Once home to early Irish kingdoms, Leinster later became the center of English power in Ireland. This history is still visible in the region’s old buildings and Georgian architecture. Leinster is rich in Irish mythology, with legends about Fionn mac Cumhaill, leprechauns, and púcaí—magical creatures that can change shape. Some people still leave a bowl of champ (mashed potatoes with scallions and butter) under a hawthorn tree as an offering to fairies. Today, Leinster remains Ireland’s most populated and economically active region.

items.name: Northern Spain
items.overview: Our Northern Spain region includes Galicia, Asturias, Cantabria, and a portion of Castile-León. Bordered to the north by the Bay of Biscay and interwoven with heavily forested mountain ranges, this segment of the Iberian Peninsula is known for fiercely resisting outside rule from a long list of invaders, including Romans and Moors. For over 1,000 years, Christian pilgrims have flocked to the rumored tomb of Saint James at Santiago de Compostela, while others have entered prehistoric caves in the Pas River Valley. From a distinct Galego language to a rich apple cider culture, this region has adapted to sometimes challenging conditions.

items.name: Crete
items.overview: Crete, the largest of the Greek islands, lies in the southern Aegean Sea. Its rugged terrain includes mountain ranges and beaches, alongside fertile valleys that support olive and grape cultivation. Crete was the heart of the Minoan civilization, whose ruins still draw visitors to sites like Knossos. Over centuries, waves of conquest left their mark, from Venetian ports to Ottoman mosques. Cretan culture is also distinct, with its own dialect, music, and dances, such as the pentozali, a lively and acrobatic dance. Despite modernization, many Cretans continue long-standing customs that reflect a proud and independent island identity rooted in history and myth.

items.name: Central Scotland & Northern Ireland
items.overview: With its center in the northern third of the island of Great Britain and crossing the North Channel to Northern Ireland, our Central Scotland & Northern Ireland region is known for its geographical beauty, medieval architecture, and folklore. Gaelic and Scots have influenced regional English dialects and are both still spoken in some areas. National symbols, including the Lion Rampant, clan tartans, and bagpipes, are often recognized internationally alongside symbols of traditional cuisine, like whisky and haggis.
items.alsoLocated: Channel Islands, England, Faroe Islands, France, Isle of Man

items.name: Southern Wales
items.overview: From the coal-rich valleys of the Rhondda to the rugged coastline of Pembrokeshire, Southern Wales helped shape Britain's industry and culture. Welsh coal miners and steelworkers were critical to Britain's Industrial Revolution. Their communities formed men's choirs that developed distinctive harmonies, building on a Celtic heritage of storytelling and song. The rolling hills of the Brecon Beacons provided Welsh lamb and local cheeses, while coastal fishing villages thrived on catches of mackerel and herring. Together, these influences combined to make Southern Wales unlike any other region in Britain.

items.name: Romania
items.overview: Romania’s diverse landscapes include dense forests, rolling hills, and river valleys that have long supported agricultural life. Once part of the Roman Empire, the region has absorbed layers of Slavic, Ottoman, and Hungarian influence. The Romanian language, rooted in Latin, distinguishes the country from its neighbors. Folklore plays a powerful role in cultural identity, and many villages still celebrate festivals with colorful costumes, carved wooden decorations, and music played on pan flutes and violins. Whether from Transylvania or Moldavia, many Romanian families keep strong ties to their roots through stories, customs, and rural traditions.

items.name: Central Italy
items.overview: Central Italy's peoples have long shown skill in making the most of available resources. More than 2,500 years ago, Etruscan farmers pioneered winemaking in Tuscany's clay hills, establishing traditions that continue to influence today’s Chianti producers. Camerino's position between the Apennine Mountains and the Adriatic Sea made it a center for banking and trade. Benedictine monks in Umbria's valleys perfected olive cultivation methods that local farmers still follow. Romans used their position on the Tiber River to control Mediterranean trade. Across the region, patterns of adaptation and innovation created communities where tradition and progress could work in tandem.

items.name: Ionian Islands
items.overview: Lying in the Ionian Sea, this group of islands—including Corfu, Lefkada, and Zakynthos—is known for its emerald hills, cypress groves, and sapphire waters. Unlike many Greek islands, the Ionian Islands were never under Ottoman control; instead, they were influenced by Venetian, French, and British rule. This history shaped the islands' elegant architecture, musical traditions, and local customs. The islands are especially known for their choral music, Easter processions, and literary heritage. Life here moves at a slower pace, often centered on family, fishing, and food, offering a distinct blend of Greek and European island culture.

items.name: Sweden
items.overview: Our Sweden region emerged from glacial ice as lands of lakes and islands, mountains and plains. Though the countries were often at war, the people share a common Norse heritage that includes elements of language, religion, and art, though they eventually developed cultures of their own. Situated along the western boundary of the Baltic Sea, relative geographic isolation did not stop the Swedes from influencing culture, trade, and politics in Europe and around the globe.

items.name: Lithuania
items.overview: Situated on the eastern edge of the Baltic Sea, Lithuania is famous for its verdant pine and birch forests and thousands of picturesque lakes. Magnificent castles are found throughout Lithuania, dating to when it was the largest country in Europe in the 14th century. Lithuania’s recent history is one of domination by powerful neighbors, particularly Russia. The occupation, executions, and forced exile of thousands of Lithuanians by the Soviet Union in the 20th century strongly shaped Lithuanians’ worldview and fierce sense of freedom. Lithuanians are avid choral singers, with the Dainų šventė—or Lithuanian Song and Dance Festival—held every four years with 30,000 performers.

items.name: Iceland
items.overview: Glaciers, geysers, and active volcanoes are just some of the geological features that make up our Iceland region. Lying just south of the Arctic Circle, the country’s beauty and ruggedness are a source of pride for its people. The island was uninhabited before the Viking age, and the vast majority of permanent settlement in Iceland took place in the late 9th and early 10th centuries. Iceland is known for its mythology, which includes supernatural beings such as gods, goddesses, elves, and trolls. While modern Icelandic society has increasing contact with the rest of Europe, Icelanders maintain their heritage through their patronymic naming system and celebrations of country’s folklore and fishing history.

items.name: North East England
items.overview: North East England is a region of rugged beauty and industry. It stretches from County Durham in the south to the Scottish border in the north, and is known for its friendly people, distinctive accents, and community spirit. The area includes the hills of County Durham, the wild landscapes of Northumberland, and the dramatic coastline along the North Sea. The Industrial Revolution made the region famous for coal mining, shipbuilding, and steel production, expanding cities like Newcastle and Sunderland. Today the North East region offers everything from the bustling city life of Newcastle to the peaceful North Pennines.

items.name: Northwestern Germany
items.overview: The coastal regions of northwest Germany have for centuries been centers for trade, fishing, and raising livestock. Once the heartland of the powerful Hanseatic League trade union, the culture-rich region now boasts major urban centers and shipping ports such as Hamburg and Bremen, as well as flat, grassy lowlands, taken back from the sea and marshes by extensive dike construction. In East Frisia, the picturesque sand dune islands, beaches, and local tea traditions attract millions of tourists each year, while the area’s unique architectural forms, such as the Low German House (Fachhallenhaus) and the Brick Gothic style, are well known.

items.name: Southern Germanic Europe
items.overview: Germany’s wealthiest and most scenic localities lie in its southernmost region, home to the German Alps and alpine lakes. It is also home to world-famous car manufacturers such as BMW and Audi, which power the economy and make the city of Munich one of the most expensive cities in Germany. Southern Germans also have a reputation for standing out culturally from other Germans. The saying “mia san mia” (“we are who we are”) expresses such pride. Southern Germans revel in their love of beer at the annual Oktoberfest fair, which showcases traditional food and drink like German pretzels and a specially brewed Wies’n Bier.

items.name: Northeastern Poland
items.overview: From its Baltic coast to its thousands of lakes and waterways, dense forests, and farmlands, our low-lying Northeastern Poland region is known today for its commitment to sustainable development and eco-tourism. Its complex history reflects centuries of shifting borders, wars, occupations, and migrations that profoundly shaped and reshaped its local populations. Today, the region’s rich culture bears traces of these many influences—from the music of the composer Frédéric Chopin to a diverse cuisine that continues to delight visitors and locals alike.

items.name: Ashkenazi Jews in Eastern Europe & Russia
items.overview: Our Eastern European & Russian Ashkenazi Jewish region focuses on communities that took shape in areas such as Poland, Latvia, Lithuania, Ukraine, Belarus, and parts of the former Russian Empire. Jews settled in these places from the Middle Ages and built strong religious and cultural traditions. Many spoke Yiddish, a language combining German, Hebrew, and Slavic words. They often lived in small towns called shtetls, where they formed close-knit communities with synagogues, schools, and charities. These Jews faced many challenges, including unfair laws, targeted violence, and later, the horrors of the Holocaust. Despite this, their traditions—such as food, music, and learning—have been passed down and are still part of Jewish life around the world today.
items.primaryLocated: Belarus, Latvia, Lithuania, Moldova, Poland, Romania, Russian, Ukraine

items.name: Estonia & Latvia
items.overview: Our Estonia & Latvia region, located along the Baltic Sea, has long served as a crossroads for trade in amber, grain, and furs, and a battleground for numerous conflicts between Scandinavians, Germans, Russians, and native peoples. Estonia has over 2,000 islands, vast forests, and Tallinn’s medieval old town. Latvia’s wide plains, deep forests, and the Daugava River shape its rich folklore. Regional specialties include verivorst (blood sausage), hearty rye bread, and silke, or herring, with baked potatoes or in a creamy soup. Estonians and Latvians have a long tradition of folk dance and singing with national festivals held every five years.

items.name: The Netherlands
items.overview: Our Netherlands region is known for its flat and low-lying geography. Less than half of the country stands over three feet above sea level, and many of its most populated areas are protected by dikes and dunes. This landscape lends itself to cycling, the preferred mode of transport of many Dutch residents, and the bicycle has become a widely-recognized symbol of the Netherlands, along with windmills, tulip fields, and wooden shoes. Dutch culture has long been characterized by an attitude of tolerance and openness, attracting persecuted religious and political minorities for centuries. Today, the Netherlands is recognized for its densely populated, modern cities such as Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and The Hague.

items.name: North Central Europe
items.overview: Our North Central Europe region combines eastern Germany, western Poland, and northern Czechia, an area shaped by successive migrations, wars, and partitions. Over the centuries, Germans, Swedes, Poles, and other Slavic peoples, and Jews have all sought the area’s vast agricultural and industrial advantages, but with sometimes devastating consequences.
