Three major river basins—the Elbe, Oder, and Vistula—connect the Baltic and North Seas to the Sudetes and Carpathian Mountains, providing fertile land, opportunities for mining and manufacturing, and key transportation and trade routes. Once the western frontier of Soviet Communist influence in Europe, the region now stands united in NATO and the European Union.

items.name: Basque
items.overview: Basque history has long been shrouded in mystery. The Basque country lies on the Bay of Biscay and in the western Pyrenees Mountains, with four provinces in Spain and three in France. The Basques have been living there longer than anyone can remember. Their language is probably the oldest in modern Europe and appears to be unrelated to any other known language in the world. Despite being an ancient people, the Basques currently have no nation of their own. They’re defined by being Basque—not by borders.

items.name: Azores
items.overview: Located in the North Atlantic Ocean, the Azores are a volcanic archipelago comprised of nine lush islands, each boasting dramatic coastlines, crater lakes, and verdant pastures. The Portuguese first settled the Azores in the 15th century. The islands became an important stop for transatlantic ships and a source of emigrants for the Americas. Today, most Azoreans live on São Miguel, the largest island. Cultural life blends Portuguese and island traditions—locals celebrate the Holy Spirit Festival with parades and feasts, tend to dairy farms, and cook traditional foods, including cozido, a stew slow-cooked underground using volcanic heat.

items.name: Ashkenazi Jews in Central & Southeastern Europe
items.overview: Our Central & Southeastern European Ashkenazi Jewish region encompasses communities of Jews who settled in this area in large numbers during the Middle Ages and Renaissance, and established centers of trade, scholarship, and communal life. Many were multilingual, speaking Yiddish and at least one other local language. Communities maintained their religious traditions through synagogues and yeshivas (religious schools). These Ashkenazi Jews contributed to urban and economic development but also faced periods of discrimination, forced conversion, and violence, including mass deportation and the deadly devastation of the Holocaust. Today, descendants of these communities live in Europe, the Americas, and South Africa, where they preserve the cultural and community ties that have been passed down through generations.
items.primaryLocated: Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Moldova, Netherlands, Poland, Serbia, Slovakia

items.name: Malta
items.overview: Our Malta region, a Mediterranean archipelago between Sicily and North Africa, comprises three inhabited islands characterized by dry, rocky terrain and sandy beaches. Over time the islands of Malta have been occupied by the Phoenicians, Greeks, Romans, and more recently the Arab and Norman Empires. It was these last two that left their trace on the Maltese language, which includes elements from Arabic, Romance languages, and English. Primarily Roman Catholic, present-day Malta most closely resembles southern Europe in its religion, culture, and architecture.

items.name: Northeastern Italy
items.overview: Northeastern Italy's prosperity comes from its productive farmland and international trade. Venice became a powerful trading center by controlling routes between Eastern markets and Europe. Venetian traders sailed to Constantinople and beyond. The Veneto region's fertile plains were ideal for growing crops, while winegrowers in the Trentino-Alto Adige region developed terraced vineyards along the steep mountainsides. The city of Trieste was Austria-Hungary's main seaport, contributing to a unique blend of Italian, Austrian, and Slavic cultures. From mountains to the sea, the geography shaped this region that has thrived on agriculture, international trade, and cultural exchange.

items.name: Eastern Czechia
items.overview: Our Eastern Czechia region is a land of rolling hills, fertile river valleys, vineyards, and mountains. Major cities include Brno, the historical capital of Moravia; Olomouc, a cosmopolitan hub on the Morava River; and Ostrava, a former industrial center near Poland. Between Olomouc and Ostrava, the Moravian Gate, a low-lying pass separating the Sudetes and Carpathian ranges, has provided a crucial corridor for trade, transportation, and migration between the Baltics and Central Europe. Contested over centuries, the region has hosted not only Moravians and Silesians but also Jews, ethnic Germans, Poles, and Slovaks, with sometimes devastating results. Today, local and national identities flourish in the region’s folk festivals, culinary traditions, and religious celebrations.

items.name: Cyprus
items.overview: Our Cyprus region is centered on an eastern Mediterranean island where rocky mountains and elevated plains slope into fertile vineyards, citrus orchards, and sandy beaches. The Phoenician, Persian, Egyptian, Roman, and Byzantine empires have each claimed the island. Today, however, after British occupation in the late 19th century and a bloody military conflict in the 1970s and 1980s, the island is politically divided between Turkish Cyprus in the north and Greek Cyprus in the south. On both sides, the people of Cyprus—known as Cypriots—have excelled at preserving traditional rural life while also building strong small-scale industries and an excellent education system.

items.name: Slovenia
items.overview: Bordered by Italy, Austria, Hungary, and Croatia, Slovenia stretches from the Alps to the Adriatic Sea. It is a small yet geographically diverse country renowned for its stunning mountains, lush forests, and picturesque lakes. Historically part of several empires and states, independence finally came in 1991. Slovenia shares cultural traits with Central Europe while maintaining a distinct Slavic identity. Slovenians celebrate seasonal festivals, preserve their local dialects, and enjoy dishes such as dumplings and hearty stews. The countryside remains dotted with traditional farmhouses and churches, often the center of community life. Slovenians value nature and sustainability.

items.name: Sephardic Jews in the Eastern Mediterranean
items.overview: Our Eastern Mediterranean Sephardic Jewish region centers on the descendants of Jews expelled from Spain and Portugal in the late 15th century, many of whom settled in parts of the Ottoman Empire, including present-day Turkey, Greece, and the Balkans. These communities preserved Judeo-Spanish (also known as Ladino), a Romance language similar to Spanish. Synagogues, schools, and other institutions developed in port cities like Thessaloniki, Istanbul, and Izmir, where Sephardic Jews played a key role in commerce and scholarship. Despite facing waves of displacement and, at times, unthinkable loss—especially during the Holocaust—many traditions remain, from religious songs and holiday foods to folk tales and proverbs passed down orally.
items.alsoLocated: Egypt, France, Italy, Libya, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain

items.name: Isle of Man
items.overview: This region, located in the Irish Sea between Great Britain and Ireland, is a British crown dependency. Inhabited since at least 6500 BCE, it has absorbed a range of cultural influences, including Gaelic, Norse, Scots, and English. This blend is reflected in the island’s folklore, in which sea gods, fairies, giants, and spirits are said to inhabit its glens and coastline. The island also maintains its own legal and political systems, including its parliament, Tynwald, which has been continuously active for at least 600 years. In addition to its unique history, mythology, and language, the Isle of Man has an active musical tradition rooted in its Celtic and Norse heritage.

items.name: Hebrides & Western Highlands, Scotland
items.overview: Our Western Highlands & Hebrides region stretches along the rugged northern Atlantic coast. Long associated with Gaelic culture, this area preserves many traditional practices, including céilidhs (informal gatherings that feature storytelling, music, and dance), and Scottish Gaelic is still spoken in parts of the Outer Hebrides. The landscape has long been shaped by sea and stone—windswept moors, peat bogs, sea lochs, and jagged cliffs. Prehistoric peoples have also left their mark with Neolithic menhirs (large stones placed upright) and Iron Age brochs (stone towers with hollow walls). Fishing and agriculture remain important, while local cuisine often features beef, seafood, and dairy products made locally.

items.name: Devon & Somerset
items.overview: The hills and coastlines of Devon and Somerset are part of England's rural heritage. This southwestern region stretches from rocky coastlines to rolling moors and lush farmlands. Rich pastures gave rise to Devon's famous clotted cream. Somerset's cider-making tradition dates back to Norman times, when monks improved ways to transform apples into alcohol. Sea trade brought exotic spices to local cooking, allowing for foods like spiced cakes and gingerbread. The region's linguistic history can be noted in Celtic place names like Exeter and Bodmin, and old Saxon words still pepper local conversations. Such cultural features are both distinctly English and uniquely southwestern.

items.name: Northern & Central Greece
items.overview: Our Northern & Central Greece region spans rugged mountains, fertile plains, and historic cities. Northern Greece includes Macedonia and Thrace, home to Mount Olympus, the legendary home of the Greek gods. Central Greece features the region of Thessaly, recognized for its rich farmland and the rock pillars of Meteora, where ancient monasteries are perched high above the ground. Cities like Thessaloniki, Greece’s second-largest city, have played a major role in trade and culture. Today, people celebrate their culture via folk music, dancing, and traditional costumes.

items.name: Munster, Ireland
items.overview: Our Munster region encompasses much of the island’s south and southwest and is home to major cities such as Cork, Limerick, and Waterford. Munster is famed for its many castles and early monasteries, including Blarney Castle and the Rock of Cashel, and for its strong traditions in Irish folk music. Many goddesses from Irish mythology—Clíodhna, Áine, and Mór Muman, to name a few—are associated with this region, as are legends like the druid-god Mug Ruith and the high king Brian Boru. Hurling, rugby, and soccer are all popular sports, and local food specialties include fresh seafood, spiced beef, and artisanal cheeses from the region’s villages and seaside towns.

items.name: Acadia
items.overview: Our Acadia region includes Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and parts of New England. It is known for its rugged shorelines, dense forests, and rolling highlands. Prior to settlement by the French in the 17th century, it was the traditional home of the Mi’kmaq people, who fished and harvested resources from the sea in warmer months and hunted moose and caribou in the cooler months. Acadia has a vibrant culture marked by lively music, French dialects, and annual festivals. Though once torn apart by colonial conflict and deportations, the Acadian identity endures proudly today, woven into the rhythms of maritime life and celebrated in the region’s cuisine and storytelling.

items.name: Connacht, Ireland
items.overview: Our Connacht region covers Ireland’s western province, including the counties of Galway, Mayo, Sligo, Leitrim, and Roscommon. Known for its stunning scenery—rugged coastlines, bogs, and mountains like the Twelve Bens and Nephin Beg—the region also has deep Gaelic roots. Irish (Gaeilge) is still spoken in Gaeltacht areas, and ancient sites like tombs and ringforts dot the landscape. Early Christian churches and towers also mark its history. Folklore plays a big role, with legends such as Queen Medb and the Fianna. Today, tourism is important, as visitors explore Connemara National Park, scenic roads, and the vibrant city of Galway.

items.name: Southern Greece
items.overview: Southern Greece, known for its rugged mountains and beautiful coastline, includes famous regions like the Peloponnese and the area around Athens. This region is the heart of ancient Greek civilization, where powerful city-states like Sparta and Corinth thrived. The Peloponnese is home to sites such as Olympia, where the first Olympic Games were held. The people of southern Greece have kept their traditions alive, including lively festivals and delicious foods like olives and feta cheese. Modern cities like Athens blend ancient ruins, such as the Parthenon, with busy streets and modern life.

items.name: Quebec
items.overview: Our Quebec region spans parts of Quebec and Ontario, as well as parts of Acadia and New England. Much of the population is concentrated along the St. Lawrence River, where cities like Montreal and Québec City thrive amid a backdrop of forests, lakes, and rolling hills. Rooted in 17th-century French colonization, the region retains a strong Francophone identity, reflected in its language laws, architecture, and cuisine. Locals might celebrate Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day with music and fireworks, enjoy poutine (a dish of french fries, cheese, and brown gravy) or tourtière (French-Canadian meat pie) or speak in the distinctive Québécois French that sets the region apart.

items.name: North East Scotland
items.overview: Our North East Scotland region stretches from the North Sea coast to the Cairngorm Mountains. The region includes the city of Aberdeen, historically known as the “Granite City.” Its hills and forests have ancient sites from the Neolithic and Bronze Ages, old Pictish stones, and medieval castles. Over time, Gaelic, Norse, and Scots cultures shaped local traditions and language. Local legends tell of kelpies, selkies, and other magical creatures said to inhabit rivers, forests, and lochs. North East Scotland is known for its seafood, beef, and whisky. Farming and fishing remain important today, thanks to good farmland and access to the sea.

items.name: Norway
items.overview: The earliest inhabitants of our Norway region were strong, seafaring peoples. For centuries, hunter-gatherers slowly pushed north across the Baltic Sea, probing coastal fjords and inland stretches for arable land as ice melted off the untamed region. While Norwegians, Swedes, and Danes all share a common Norse heritage, over time, Norway’s resilient coastal communities evolved into a nation known for its seamanship, technology, artistry, and mythology.

items.name: Southern Poland
items.overview: Our Southern Poland region is the historical and cultural heart of Poland, with its well-preserved ancient capital, Kraków. The region’s natural beauty stretches across the Polish uplands, the Vistula glacial valley, and several mountain ranges, including the Holy Cross (Świętokrzyskie) Mountains and the towering Tatra and Beskid (Bieszczady) Mountains in the Carpathian range bordering Slovakia. Cultural highlights include the wooden churches of the Carpathian highlanders, the world-famous Wieliczka Salt Mine, pre-World War II synagogues, and Oskar Schindler’s enamel factory in Kraków.

items.name: Portugal
items.overview: Geography contributed to the separate people, language, and nation-state that lie at the heart of our Portugal region. The country of Portugal shares its northern and eastern borders with Spain on the western edge of the Iberian Peninsula. Mountains in the north give way to rolling plains in the south, while the Atlantic to the west and south led to a seafaring tradition that enabled the Portuguese to establish a trading empire that circled the globe.

items.name: Germans in Russia
items.overview: Our Germans in Russian region refers to the thousands of ethnic Germans who emigrated to the Russian Empire in the 18th and 19th centuries in return for free land, no taxes for 30 years, and political autonomy. Settling in the fertile Volga and Black Sea regions, the migrants successfully maintained their German identity for 200 years. Russian-Germans were known for their craftsmanship, including the J. Höhn factory in Odessa, the largest plow manufacturer in Russia. In the 20th century, war between Germany and the Soviet Union led to intense persecution of Russian Germans, with close to one million perishing in executions, famines, and war. The majority of Russian Germans chose to return to Germany when the Soviet Union collapsed.

items.name: Madeira
items.overview: Located in the North Atlantic Ocean, the Madeira archipelago consists of four islands—Madeira, Porto Santo, and the largely uninhabited islands of Desertas and Selvagens. Known for steep cliffs, terraced hillsides, and subtropical forests, the islands were settled by the Portuguese in the 15th century and played a key role in Atlantic trade. Today, most people live on the main island of Madeira, in and around the capital, Funchal. Locals celebrate their culture with lively flower and wine festivals, explore mountain paths that follow historic levadas (irrigation channels), and enjoy traditional island food like bolo do caco (flatbreads) and espetada (skewers).
items.alsoLocated: Brazil, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Spain, Venezuela

items.name: Tonga
items.overview: More than 160 islands comprise the Kingdom of Tonga. Our Tonga region is centered on the 36 that are inhabited. The islands are known for their picturesque coral reefs, limestone cliffs, sandy beaches, and occasional volcanic activity. The only monarchy in the South Pacific, Tonga’s royal family predates European arrival by centuries, and Tonga has never been colonized by Europeans. Traditional Tongan culture includes dance, mythology, weaving, and woodcarving. The ritual drinking of kava, produced from the roots of a pepper plant, is common throughout the region, which extends to Samoa, Fiji, Kiribati, and Micronesia.
items.alsoLocated: Fiji, Kiribati, Papua New Guinea, Samoa, Solomon Islands

items.name: Melanesia
items.overview: Including Papua New Guinea and the island chains of the Bismarck and Solomon Archipelagos, our Melanesia region is home to some of the worlds' best-preserved primitive societies. The ancient populations of Melanesia remained mostly separated from the rest of the world for tens of thousands of years. A combination of geographical isolation, rugged terrain, and few crops and animals suitable for domestication led to the perpetuation of ancient technology and culture.
items.primaryLocated: East Timor, Fiji, New Caledonia, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu

items.name: Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples
items.overview: The Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples region spans across Australia’s varied landscapes and surrounding islands. As the first peoples of Australia, they predate European settlement and colonization by tens of thousands of years. Though the exact date is unknown, current research approximates that Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander groups have been living on this continent for at least 60,000 years. Within this region, each individual community (whether family group, clan, or nation) is connected to their own ancestral homeland(s), each of which has its own combination of place, language, and culture.

items.name: Samoa
items.overview: Our Samoa region extends outward from the islands of Samoa. Many of these islands have been inhabited for at least 3,000 years, and residents of Samoa have had contact with Fijians and Tongans for centuries. This region of Oceania is largely characterized by its tropical volcanic islands, Polynesian culture and cuisine, and the practice of Christianity. Agriculture, including breadfruit, taro, and pineapples, constitutes one of the region’s major industries, along with fishing and tourism. Culturally, the region is famed for its unique music, dance, and tattoo artistry.
items.alsoLocated: Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Tonga

items.name: Guam
items.overview: The densely forested volcanic island at the heart of our Guam region lies about 1,500 miles east of the Philippines in the northern Pacific Ocean and boasts coral reefs, steep cliffs, and a tropical climate. Guam was originally settled over 3,000 years ago by the Chamorro people, who named the island “Guåhan,” which loosely translates as “ours.” A long history of colonization by Spain, the U.S., and Japan has given it a uniquely blended culture that includes Chamorro traditions such as the Bailan Lina’la’ dance and folklore surrounding taotaomo’na, the island’s ancestral spirits.

items.name: New Zealand Maori
items.overview: Our New Zealand Māori region is centered around New Zealand’s two main islands and stretches northeast across the South Pacific to include the Cook Islands and Easter Island. In total, the region covers a vast portion of the South Pacific Ocean, but just over 100,000 square miles of land, much of which is characterized by volcanic islands and coral atolls. The Māori are thought to have first arrived in New Zealand 700 years ago and were the first humans to inhabit this remote part of the world. The expert boatbuilding and seafaring abilities that allowed them to make their home in New Zealand have persisted through the centuries, as have other cultural elements unique to Polynesia, including ceremonial dances, tattoo artistry, and the Māori language, which gave English the word “kiwi,” which is both the name of New Zealand’s national bird and its national fruit.

items.name: Hawaii
items.overview: Our Hawaii region includes the 137 islands of the Hawaiian archipelago, as well as the Cook Islands, Easter Island, and the other volcanic islands and coral atolls that constitute Eastern Polynesia. In total, the region comprises several hundred landmasses scattered across the Pacific Ocean, making it easy to see why it was named “Polynesia,” from the Greek for “many islands.” Hawaii’s first settlers are thought to have arrived by boat from Tahiti between 1,300 and 1,600 years ago. Although remote, inhabitants of the Hawaiian Islands were likely not isolated from other Pacific civilizations thanks to their long history as expert seafarers, and evidence of ties to other Polynesian islands can be seen in the similarities of their ceremonial dances, wood carvings, and practice of surfing. Today, Hawaii is characterized by its ethnic and cultural diversity stemming from centuries of immigration from parts of North America, East Asia, Europe, and other Polynesian islands.
